title: Checkpoint: Personality and Wellbeing
objective: After this level you can explain how traits, appraisals and habits shape how people cope and thrive.
summary: Traits predict life outcomes about as well as family background and ability, while appraisals and habits are the day-to-day levers of coping and thriving.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: who you are, how you judge, what you repeat.
cards.body: This chapter moved from the traits you carry, to the judgments you make under stress, to the habits you build. First, a test of whether traits matter much at all; then the chapter's three levers side by side.

cards.fact: Traits predicted death, divorce and career success about as well as socioeconomic status and cognitive ability.
cards.context: In 2007, Brent Roberts and colleagues reviewed only prospective studies, which follow people over time, and tried to limit the review to studies that controlled for background factors. Traits predicted mortality, divorce and job attainment about as well as socioeconomic status and cognitive ability. Like every finding in this chapter, it describes groups, not one person's fate.

learned: How traits, appraisals and habits each shape the way people cope and thrive.
Why psychologists measure personality on sliding scales instead of sorting people into types.

questions.prompt: Personality and Wellbeing recap: in the 2007 review, how did traits compare with socioeconomic status and cognitive ability at predicting divorce?

options.label: About as well as the other two
Far better than both combined
options.rationale: The effects were about the same size.

options.label: Only for people over 70
options.rationale: The review covered outcomes across adult life.

questions.explanation: Traits predicted mortality, divorce and job attainment about as well as socioeconomic status and cognitive ability.

questions.prompt: Personality and Wellbeing recap: why do dial-style trait scores hold steadier on retest than four-letter types?

options.label: Trait tests ask far fewer questions
options.rationale: The number of questions isn't the reason.

options.label: People near the middle stay near the middle, with no cut-off to flip
Trait tests are taken only once in life
options.rationale: Retests show trait scores stay closely matched.

options.label: Types measure a different, faster-changing personality

questions.explanation: Most people score near the middle. Types split scales at a cut-off, so small shifts flip letters; dials just record a nearby score.

questions.prompt: Personality and Wellbeing recap, from Level 84: what is the Flynn effect?

options.label: Average IQ scores rising across generations
IQ scores falling as people age
IQ fully explaining school grades
options.rationale: IQ explains only about a quarter of grade differences.

options.label: Brothers always scoring identically
options.rationale: The Norwegian study used brothers to test causes.

questions.explanation: The Flynn effect is the rise in average IQ scores, about three points per decade, across the 20th century.

questions.prompt: Personality and Wellbeing recap, from Level 87: after the September 11 attacks, what did most New York-area residents in the large 2006 study show?

options.label: Delayed grief after a year
options.rationale: The study measured the first six months.

options.label: No reaction because they felt nothing

questions.explanation: About 65 percent were resilient, and resilience never fell below about a third of any group.

questions.prompt: Personality and Wellbeing recap, from Level 86: when a stressor truly can't be changed, which coping tends to fit best?

options.label: Avoiding all coping
options.rationale: Coping still helps when a stressor can't be changed.

options.label: Changing the stressor anyway
options.rationale: By definition, it can't be changed.

questions.explanation: People lean on emotion-focused coping for stressors they feel powerless to change, and the goodness-of-fit idea says that match helps.
